title: What is Cross-Validation?
description: How K-fold, leave-p-out and leave-one-out splits estimate model performance, and how chain and sliding window validation handle time series.
content:
**Cross-validation** is a technique used to evaluate a model by partitioning the dataset into subsets. Instead of relying on a single train-test split, the model is trained and validated multiple times on different partitions of the data, which makes the estimate of its performance more reliable.

Common cross-validation schemes:
• K-fold cross-validation
• Leave-p-out cross-validation
• Leave-one-out cross-validation
• Chain cross-validation (for time series)
• Sliding window validation (for time series)

K-fold cross-validation: the dataset is separated into K folds. The model is trained on K − 1 folds and validated on the remaining one. This process is repeated K times, so each fold serves as a validation dataset exactly once.

Leave-p-out cross-validation: in each iteration, p samples are held out as the validation set, while the model is trained on the rest of the data. Its special case is leave-one-out cross-validation, where each fold is the size of one (p = 1), so the model is validated on every single sample separately.

Computational cost matters here: as the number of folds increases, the computational load increases linearly - there are as many training iterations as there are folds. That is why K-fold cross-validation is faster than leave-p-out cross-validation, which requires far more training iterations.

An effective approach to apply cross-validation in the realm of time series analysis is chain cross-validation: the model is iteratively trained on a subset of data and validated on the next data record, while the training subset keeps increasing. This respects the order of observations - the model is always validated on data that comes after its training data.

A variation of chain cross-validation is the sliding window approach: after each iteration, the train and test window is moved forward by a fixed number of time steps, so the model always trains on a window of a fixed length.
